title: Effects of ginger intervention on anthropometric and body composition indices in patients with type 2 diabetes: a GRADE-assessed systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

grader.main_outcome: body mass index and body fat percentage
grader.population: adults with type 2 diabetes

label: approved
note: BMI pooled MD written '- 0.24' with a space after the minus; BF% also a main outcome; limitation: risk of bias in most trials.
abstract:
Background and aims

Evidence on the effects of ginger supplementation on anthropometric and body composition indices in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is inconsistent, and the certainty of this evidence has not been fully evaluated. This study aimed to systematically review and meta-analyze randomized controlled trials assessing these effects.

Methods

PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched until October 5, 2025. We used random-effects meta-analysis to find average differences with 95% CIs. Study quality and evidence certainty were checked with Cochrane RoB-2 tool and GRADE approach. Subgroup, meta-regression, sensitivity, and publication bias analyses were also done.

Results

This meta-analysis included 692 participants from 12 RCTs. Ginger supplementation significantly reduced body mass index (BMI) (- 0.24 kg/m²; 95% CI: -0.48, - 0.00; p = 0.043) and body fat percentage (BF%) (- 1.44%; 95% CI: -2.49, - 0.38; p = 0.007), while no significant effects were observed on body weight (BW), waist circumference (WC), hip circumference (HC), or waist-to-hip ratio (WHR). Bias assessment showed 9 studies with some concerns, 1 low, and 2 high risk. Evidence quality was moderate for 4 outcomes (BMI, WHR, HC, BF%), low for WC, and high for BW.

Conclusion

Ginger reduced BMI and BF%, with no significant change in BW, WHR, HC, or WC.

Trial registration

This study was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251162956).

title: Park renovations in low-income New York City neighborhoods and changes in adult physical activity and sedentary behavior: a quasi-experimental study.

grader.main_outcome: accelerometer-measured physical activity and sedentary time
grader.population: adults living within 0.3 miles of parks in low-income New York City neighborhoods

label: approved
note: Renovation effect not significant, no estimate; the numbers given are for park-use subgroups.
abstract:
Background

Inadequate physical activity (PA) elevates chronic disease risk in low-income urban populations. Neighborhood parks may offer venues for PA, but effects likely depend on park quality and use patterns. This study examined whether citywide park renovations were associated with changes in adult PA and sedentary behavior (SB) in low-income New York City neighborhoods and whether associations between park use and PA/SB changes differed for residents near renovated vs. control parks.

Methods

We conducted a quasi‑experimental prospective cohort study (2016-2022) in neighborhoods surrounding 31 renovated and 21 matched control parks. Participants included 344 adults living ≤ 0.3 miles of a study park (186 intervention, 158 control). Outcomes were accelerometry‑based PA/SB measures collected pre‑ and post‑renovation: vector magnitude per minute (VMPM) and minutes/day of sedentary time, light PA, and moderate‑to‑vigorous PA. Surveys assessed self‑reported typical frequency and duration of park visits. Linear mixed‑effects difference-in-differences models estimated associations between renovations and PA/SB changes; interaction models examined associations of park use with PA/SB changes in intervention vs. control groups.

Results

Changes in PA/SB were not significantly different between intervention and control groups. However, intervention participants who reported visiting their study park ≥ 30 min on a weekend day experienced a 140.0-unit/day greater increase in VMPM (95% CI 52.7,227.2) and a 61.1-minute/day larger decrease in sedentary time (95% CI -108.8,-13.3) compared to those with shorter visit durations. Furthermore, in the intervention group, each additional 60 min spent at a study park on weekdays was associated with 18.0 more minutes/day of light PA (95% CI 4.7,31.3), and each additional 60 min spent at the study park on weekend days corresponded to 19.0 more minutes/day of light PA (95% CI 8.1,29.9) and a 54.1-unit increase in VMPM/day (95% CI 7.5,100.7). No associations between park use duration and PA/SB changes were observed in the control group.

Conclusions

Park renovations alone were not associated with PA/SB changes, but longer duration of visits at renovated-but not control-parks were associated with increased total PA volume and light PA, and decreased sedentary time. High-quality park environments may be a necessary pre-condition to the benefits of park use on adult PA/SB.

title: Dapagliflozin attenuates progression from prefrailty to frailty in patients with hypertension and chronic kidney disease.

grader.main_outcome: progression from prefrailty to frailty at 1 year
grader.population: hypertensive adults over 65 with chronic kidney disease and prefrailty

label: approved
note: OR 0.130 with 'CI 0.045-0.381' but no stated level, so no interval.
abstract: BACKGROUNDChronic kidney disease (CKD) and hypertension share common pathophysiological pathways contributing to vascular damage, endothelial dysfunction, and physical decline, particularly in older adults with prefrailty. To evaluate the relationship among renal injury, physical performance, and frailty progression in hypertensive older adults with CKD and assess whether dapagliflozin associates with reduced frailty progression, we designed the study DAPA-FORTRESS (DAPAgliflozin and Frailty prOgression in hypeRTension and chRonic kidnEy diSeaSe).METHODSWe enrolled 135 prefrail hypertensive patients with CKD aged >65 years and followed them for 1 year. After coarsened exact matching, our balanced cohort had 105 patients (52 dapagliflozin). Associations between albuminuria, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and physical performance were analyzed using correlation and regression models. Effect of dapagliflozin on frailty progression was evaluated using multivariable logistic regression.RESULTSA significant inverse association between gait speed and albuminuria (r2 = 0.48, P < 0.0001) and significant positive linear association between gait speed and eGFR (r2 = 0.18; P < 0.0001) were observed. Patients with eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 exhibited significantly worse physical performance than those with higher eGFR (P = 0.0003). In adjusted analyses, receiving dapagliflozin was independently associated with lower odds of progressing to frailty at 1 year (OR = 0.130; CI 0.045-0.381; P < 0.001).CONCLUSIONIn older hypertensive patients with CKD, greater renal injury is associated with worse physical performance, while dapagliflozin use reduces the risk of frailty progression. These findings indicate a potential protective role of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibition in mitigating functional decline in this high-risk population.FUNDINGNIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (R01-HL146691), National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (R01-DK123259); American Heart Association (AHA- 24IPA1268813, AHA-22-915561, AHA-24-1195524).

title: Six-Month Music Practice Versus Psychomotor Interventions in Mild Cognitive Impairment: Behavioral and Hippocampal Outcomes.

grader.main_outcome: global cognition and hippocampal functional connectivity
grader.population: adults with mild cognitive impairment

label: approved
note: No numbers; pilot, preliminary findings.
abstract: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is characterized by measurable cognitive decline with largely preserved daily functioning and increased risk of dementia. MCI patients may also exhibit sensorimotor and communication impairments, while hippocampal atrophy and altered functional connectivity are prominent neural features associated with further cognitive decline. Evidence from nonpharmacological interventions integrating cognitive challenge, coordinated movement, and emotional engagement remains limited in early-stage MCI. In this pilot intervention study, we examined whether 6 months of intensive musical instrument training versus psychomotor interventions were associated with changes in cognitive and sensorimotor performance, hippocampal gray matter volume, and functional connectivity. Outcomes were compared between randomized MCI groups, with matched healthy controls as reference for test-retest and age-related neural effects. Improvements in global cognition were modest, reaching marginal significance only in the music group, while both interventions were associated with complementary domain-specific cognitive and sensorimotor gains. Hippocampal gray matter volume remained stable across all three groups, whereas hippocampal functional connectivity declined in healthy controls but remained stable in both intervention groups, consistent with possible functional neural maintenance. These preliminary findings suggest that group-based, low-risk music and psychomotor interventions may support cognitive, sensorimotor, and neural functioning in early MCI, warranting further investigation in larger controlled trials.

title: Obesity-a key driver in osteoarthritis.

grader.main_outcome: WOMAC pain and function scores after 2 years by weight change
grader.population: adults with knee osteoarthritis who are overweight or obese, from a randomised trial

label: approved
note: Within-group WOMAC changes by weight change, no between-group difference.
abstract:
Purpose

Obesity causes mechanical stress and metabolic dysfunction. However, the relationship between obesity and osteoarthritis (OA) pain still needs further investigation. This study aims to examine the effect of weight loss on pain and function through a secondary analysis of a randomized, double-blind, multicenter OA trial and to evaluate obesity's impact on OA pain using a rat model.

Methods

In a post hoc analysis of a randomized controlled trial (RCT; NCT00486434), we evaluated baseline body mass index and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis (WOMAC) scores (n = 1175) and examined the impact of 5% weight loss on WOMAC scores after 2 years using a factorial analysis of covariance (n = 674). In a preclinical model of metabolic OA induced by meniscectomy, pain-like behavior was assessed with the von Frey and cold plate tests.

Results

Participants who lost >5% of weight within 2 years experienced a mean decrease of -567.1 (95% CI -666.7 to -467.6) and -399.2 (-505.8 to -292.5) in total WOMAC scores for their target and nontarget knees, respectively, whereas individuals who gained >5% in weight had a smaller decrease of -364.6 (-496.5 to -232.7) and -135 (-277.4 to -6.3), respectively. Additionally, the high-fat diet-fed rat model showed more pain-like behavior than the lean model.

Main conclusion

These studies indicate that weight loss could decrease OA pain in both target and nontarget knees of patients with obesity, supporting the inclusion of obesity in OA animal models to improve the translatability of OA treatments.

title: Comparative efficacy of different exercise modalities on renal function and glycemic control in patients with non-dialysis diabetic kidney disease: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.

grader.main_outcome: estimated glomerular filtration rate and glycated hemoglobin
grader.population: adults with non-dialysis diabetic kidney disease

label: approved
note: eGFR, resistance training vs usual care; HbA1c MD -1.65% has no interval; limitation: fragile to bias, sparse safety monitoring.
abstract:
Objective

To evaluate the comparative efficacy and safety of structured exercise modalities on renal function and glycemic control in non-dialysis diabetic kidney disease (DKD).

Design

Systematic review and network meta-analysis.

Data sources

Six databases (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang) were searched from inception to July 15, 2026.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating structured exercise (aerobic, resistance, combined, or mind-body) versus usual care or an active comparator in adults with non-dialysis DKD (duration ≥4 weeks).

Outcome measures

Renal endpoints were estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and urinary albumin excretion (UAE); glycemic endpoints were glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) and fasting blood glucose (FBG).

Results

Twenty RCTs (1,746 patients) were included. Compared with usual care, resistance training (RT) was the sole modality significantly increasing eGFR (mean difference [MD] 11.36 mL/min/1.73 m², 95% CI 4.47 to 18.25; low certainty) and outperforming aerobic training (MD 8.61, 2.22 to 15.00). Mind-body exercise (MBE) was the only intervention significantly reducing UAE (standardized mean difference -1.41, -2.67 to -0.16; low certainty). For glycemic regulation, RT (MD -1.65%), aerobic training (MD -1.07%), and combined training (CT; MD -0.70%) significantly lowered HbA1c (all low certainty). Significant FBG reductions occurred only with RT (MD -1.78 mmol/L; low certainty) and CT (MD -1.71 mmol/L; moderate certainty). In sensitivity analyses, RT's eGFR benefit lost significance after excluding high-risk trials (MD 8.24, -1.17 to 17.64), and CT's HbA1c reduction was attenuated in pure-exercise models (MD -0.60%, -1.39 to 0.19). Subgroup analyses showed CT uniquely sustained FBG reductions across short-term (≤12 weeks: MD -1.50) and longer-term (>12 weeks: MD -2.39) regimens. Structured safety was monitored in only five trials (25.0%): three reported mild, transient events without serious harm, while two explicitly declared zero adverse events. Thus, current evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions regarding comparative safety.

Conclusions

Structured exercise confers distinct adaptations in non-dialysis DKD. Combined training provides a reliable foundation for sustained glycemic management, while mind-body exercise represents a viable strategy for albuminuria. Resistance training's apparent renal benefit warrants caution due to fragility against bias. Prescriptions should be individualized rather than seeking a single optimal modality. Given the sparse monitoring of adverse events, comparative clinical safety cannot be definitively established and mandates routine surveillance.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420261489091.

title: Bedside Bioimpedance and Simple Functional Tests Identify Muscle Function Impairment Predicting Overall Survival in Chemotherapy-treated Metastatic Urothelial Carcinoma: A Retrospective Pilot Study.

grader.main_outcome: overall survival
grader.population: adults with metastatic urothelial carcinoma treated with systemic chemotherapy

label: approved
note: No numbers.
abstract:
Objectives

To evaluate whether bedside bioimpedance analysis and simple functional tests can identify muscle function impairment associated with overall survival in chemotherapy-treated metastatic urothelial carcinoma.

Materials

Retrospective single-center observational cohort study.

Methods

We reviewed 56 consecutive patients treated with systemic chemotherapy between January 2014 and February 2021. Skeletal muscle index was estimated using bioimpedance analysis. Handgrip strength and walking speed were assessed in routine care. Sarcopenia-related categories were defined using sex-specific Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia thresholds. The prespecified primary comparison was reference (normal plus pre-sarcopenia) versus muscle function impairment (dynapenia plus sarcopenia). Overall survival was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox models with minimal age adjustment.

Results

Muscle function impairment was associated with shorter overall survival compared with the reference group. The association remained after age adjustment. Baseline characteristics suggested greater vulnerability in the impairment group, including lower body weight and serum albumin and higher inflammatory burden.

Conclusions

A pragmatic bedside phenotype based on bioimpedance analysis and simple functional testing may help identify chemotherapy-treated metastatic urothelial carcinoma patients at higher risk of poor survival.

title: Recreational football as medicine? A meta-analysis of its effects and feasibility in patients with chronic diseases.

grader.main_outcome: body fat percentage and cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2peak) in chronic disease populations
grader.population: adolescents and adults with selected chronic diseases

label: approved
note: Body fat % SMD, lower limit written '- 0.57'; VO2peak also a main outcome; limitation: heterogeneity, low certainty.
abstract:
Objective

To quantitatively synthesise the effects of recreational football interventions on physiological and feasibility-related outcomes in people with chronic diseases.

Methods

PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 6 February 2026, and additional searches of Scopus and Embase were conducted on 17 August 2026. Controlled trials of recreational football in adolescents and adults with selected chronic disease populations were eligible. Three-level random-effects meta-analyses were performed, with cluster-robust (CR2) variance estimation, clustering on the independent trial, applied to every outcome as a robustness check, and certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE.

Results

Twenty-two study reports representing 17 unique trials (15 randomised and 2 non-randomised controlled trials; 588 unique participants) were included. Recreational football was associated with significant improvements in body fat percentage (k = 13; SMD = -0.36, 95% CI - 0.57 to -0.14; p < 0.01), muscle mass (k = 12; SMD = 0.22, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.44; p = 0.05), diastolic blood pressure (k = 12; SMD = -0.53, 95% CI - 0.96 to -0.09; p = 0.02), mean arterial pressure (k = 7; SMD = -0.89, 95% CI - 1.48 to -0.29; p = 0.01), resting heart rate (k = 10; SMD = -1.01, 95% CI - 1.72 to -0.31; p = 0.01), VO₂peak (k = 16; SMD = 0.70, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.03; p < 0.01), Yo-Yo Intermittent Endurance Test level 1 performance (k = 4; SMD = 1.43, 95% CI 0.83 to 2.03; p < 0.01), triglycerides (k = 11; SMD = -0.56, 95% CI - 0.91 to -0.22; p < 0.01), total cholesterol (k = 11; SMD = -0.69, 95% CI - 1.08 to -0.30; p < 0.01), plasma osteocalcin (k = 4; SMD = 1.07, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.60; p < 0.01), and P1NP (k = 4; SMD = 1.28, 95% CI 0.22 to 2.34; p = 0.03). Borderline effects that were not retained under cluster-robust inference were observed for fat mass (SMD = -0.30; p = 0.05), systolic blood pressure (SMD = -0.60; p = 0.05) and LDL (SMD = -0.50; p = 0.05). No statistically significant pooled effects were observed for body weight (SMD = -0.29; p = 0.05), BMI (SMD = -0.06; p = 0.71), waist circumference (SMD = -0.48; p = 0.18), HbA1c (SMD = -0.28; p = 0.10), fasting glucose (SMD = -0.11; p = 0.48), fasting insulin (SMD = 0.07; p = 0.73), HDL (SMD = 0.10; p = 0.70), CRP (SMD = -0.88; p = 0.13), DXA-derived leg and whole-body bone mineral density or content (all p ≥ 0.11), or CTX-1 (SMD = 0.54; p = 0.19). Effects on body fat percentage, fat mass, muscle mass, SBP and LDL were sensitive to the assumed pre-post correlation. Under cluster-robust (CR2) inference the statistical interpretation was unchanged for 22 of the 27 outcomes; fat mass, SBP, LDL and P1NP were no longer significant (all p between 0.05 and 0.07) and whole-body bone mineral density became significant (p = 0.03). Certainty of evidence was low to very low for most outcomes, and adverse events were summarized narratively because quantitative synthesis was not possible. Mean attendance was 82.7% across 13 independent trials, and mean attrition was 15.6% across 14 independent trials.

Conclusion

Across the selected chronic disease populations represented in the current evidence base, recreational football showed signals of potential benefit for cardiorespiratory fitness and selected cardiovascular, lipid, and bone-related outcomes, although adiposity- and bone-formation-related effects were less robust in sensitivity analyses. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously due to heterogeneity and generally low or very low certainty of evidence. Recreational football may be considered a supervised adjunctive exercise option.

title: Photobiomodulation for radiotherapy-induced dysgeusia in head and neck cancer patients: a pilot randomized clinical trial.

grader.main_outcome: taste identification (dysgeusia) during radiotherapy
grader.population: adults with head and neck cancer undergoing radiotherapy

label: approved
note: Proportions per group, p > 0.05; pilot, preliminary.
abstract: Dysgeusia is a frequent complication in patients with head and neck cancer (HNC) undergoing radiotherapy and may negatively affect nutritional status and quality of life. This pilot study evaluated the effect of photobiomodulation (PBM) on the management of radiotherapy-induced dysgeusia. Sixteen patients undergoing radiotherapy for HNC were randomly assigned to either a PBM group (n = 8) or a zinc sulfate group (n = 8). Objective taste identification tests evaluating sweet, bitter, sour, and salty tastes were performed at three time points: before radiotherapy (T0), at the 15th radiotherapy session (T1), and at the 30th radiotherapy session (T2). Salty taste was the most affected taste modality in both groups. At T2, sweet taste was correctly identified by 75.0% of patients in the zinc group and 50.0% in the PBM group. In contrast, bitter taste was preserved in 87.5% of patients in the PBM group and 75.0% in the zinc group. Sour taste was preserved in 87.5% and 62.5% of patients in the PBM and zinc groups, respectively, whereas salty taste was preserved in 50.0% and 25.0% of patients, respectively. No statistically significant differences were observed between groups at T0, T1, or T2 (all p > 0.05). Although no statistically significant differences were identified, PBM was associated with better preservation of sour, bitter, and salty taste perception, particularly after the 30th radiotherapy session. These preliminary findings suggest that PBM may represent a promising supportive strategy for the management of treatment-related dysgeusia in patients with HNC undergoing radiotherapy.

abstract:
Background and objective

Frailty is associated with muscle weakness, impaired physical function, and increased risk of disability and loss of independence, making preservation of muscle function an important public health goal for healthy aging. Resistance training may help address these deficits, but its effects in frail or pre-frail older adults remain uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated its effects on muscle strength, physical function, and frailty score.

Methods

Seven electronic information sources were searched from inception to August 2026, with no language restrictions. Randomized controlled trials were included if they enrolled adults aged ≥60 years who were clearly diagnosed as frail or pre-frail using validated tools or comprehensive assessments. The intervention was limited to structured resistance training without combination with other exercise modalities. Random-effects models were used for meta-analysis, and the certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach.

Results

Nine randomized controlled trials comprising 27 study arms and 566 participants were included. Low-certainty evidence suggested that resistance training may improve knee extensor strength (SMD = 1.30, 95% CI: 0.48 to 2.13). Very-low-certainty evidence showed possible improvements in handgrip strength (MD = 4.15 kg, 95% CI: 0.81 to 7.48) and gait speed (MD = 0.13 m/s, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.26), whereas the effects on Timed Up and Go (TUG), Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) and frailty score remained uncertain. For handgrip strength, gait speed, TUG, and SPPB, clinical importance remained uncertain because the 95% CI encompassed the corresponding reference thresholds for clinical importance. Between-study heterogeneity was substantial to considerable.

Conclusion

Resistance training may improve knee extensor strength and may also benefit handgrip strength and gait speed in frail or pre-frail older adults, although the certainty of evidence is low to very low; effects on TUG, SPPB, and frailty score remain uncertain. Because muscle weakness and functional decline contribute to disability and loss of independence in later life, these findings may inform resistance-training strategies aimed at supporting muscle health and healthy aging. Further high-quality trials with standardized training prescriptions and longer-term follow-up are needed.

title: Potential Health Benefits of Piceatannol-Rich Extracts from <i>Passiflora edulis</i> f. <i>flavicarpa</i> Seeds on Modulating Gene Expressions Related to Fat Metabolism and Muscle Development in C2C12 Myotubes.

grader.main_outcome: gene expression related to fat metabolism and muscle development in C2C12 myotubes

label: approved
note: Cells; no effect numbers.
abstract: Yellow passion fruits are widely cultivated in many countries. Throughout industrial manufacturing operations, seeds are frequently disposed of as byproducts. Passion fruit seeds are an abundant natural source of piceatannol, which is known for its antioxidant properties and its ability to modulate protein turnover. This study investigated the potential benefits of passion fruit (PF) extract from pulp and juice, as well as piceatannol-rich (PIC) extract from passion fruit seeds, on palmitic acid (PA)-induced myosteatosis-related muscle atrophy in C2C12 myotubes at the transcriptional level. The PIC extract yielded 5.1% (w/w) with a piceatannol concentration of 0.37% (w/w). The result showed that the PIC extract was more effective in free radical scavenging than the piceatannol standard. Additionally, the results demonstrated that PA promoted lipid accumulation while impairing the muscle formation and glucose absorption. However, both PF and PIC extracts demonstrated a significant reduction in PA-induced lipid accumulation, accompanied by suppression of diacylglycerol acyltransferase 1 (Dgat1) expression without altering sirtuin 1 (Sirt1) and uncoupling protein 3 (Ucp3). In addition, both extracts tended to enhance the expression of myosin heavy chain 1 (Myh1) and glucose transporter type 4 (GLUT4), while markedly reducing myostatin (Mstn) expression, suggesting improvements in muscle development and glucose uptake. Furthermore, the PIC extract suppressed pancreatic lipase activity, which minimizes spikes in postprandial triglycerides in the blood circulation of rats. These findings emphasize the potential health benefits of PF and PIC extracts in enhancing glucose absorption and inhibiting fat synthesis in C2C12 myotubes, suggesting potential to mitigate lipid accumulation-related muscle development. The promising findings from cell culture suggest further in vivo investigation for studying their physiological relevance to muscle wasting caused by fat accumulation in obesity.

title: Adults With Type 1 Diabetes Are Less Physically Active Than Adults Without Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

grader.main_outcome: total physical activity
grader.population: adults with type 1 diabetes compared with adults without diabetes

label: approved
note: Total physical activity, Hedges g, type 1 diabetes vs none; generalisability limited.
abstract:
Aims

Physical activity is central to the management of type 1 diabetes, yet diabetes-specific barriers may reduce habitual activity. We systematically reviewed and meta-analysed studies comparing physical activity and sedentary behaviour in adults with type 1 diabetes and adults without diabetes.

Material and methods

MEDLINE, Embase, and SPORTDiscus were searched from inception to 24 July 2026. Random-effects models were used to pool standardised mean differences for continuous outcomes and odds ratios (OR) for meeting physical activity recommendations or study-defined active criteria.

Results

Sixteen publications representing 14 independent cohorts and 3335 participants were included (54.2% females). Adults with type 1 diabetes had lower total physical activity than adults without diabetes (12 studies; Hedges g = -0.13; 95% confidence interval, -0.22 to -0.05; p = 0.001), with no detected heterogeneity. They also had lower estimated odds of meeting a physical activity criterion, although the association was not statistically significant (4 studies; OR = 0.77; 95% confidence interval, 0.58-1.02; p = 0.066). Mean age, diabetes duration and glycated haemoglobin were not associated with between-group differences in total physical activity. Data were insufficient to pool sedentary behaviour, steps or intensity-specific outcomes.

Conclusions

Adults with type 1 diabetes engage in slightly less total physical activity than adults without diabetes, although evidence regarding adherence to physical activity recommendations remains inconclusive. The absence of population-based studies limits the generalisability of these findings and highlights the need for representative studies using standardised device-based assessments.

title: A systematic review of Moringa oleifera seed toxicity and safety: Comparative analysis of toxicology methodologies and results.

grader.main_outcome: acute and sub-acute oral toxicity (LD50 and NOAEL) of Moringa oleifera seeds in rodents
grader.population: rodents exposed to Moringa oleifera seed in toxicity tests

label: approved
note: Narrative synthesis of rodent toxicity tests; safety limits unreliable.
abstract: This systematic review aims to assess the reliability of contemporary toxicological research on Moringa oleifera seeds. Academic databases were browsed on a yearly basis (2014-2024); identification and screening were conducted between July 17th 2023 and January 13th 2025. Primary research reports on M. oleifera seed toxicology were included for data collection. Fifty-three fields were used to collect data. Data was synthesised by comparing methodological data points to contemporary toxicity testing guidelines; results were presented as a narrative synthesis. Conflict of interest, research quality and risk of bias were assessed using Cochrane tools modified for non-human laboratory studies. Thirty-seven non-duplicate publications were identified, of which 14 were included for data collection. In total, 395 data points were collected and synthesised. Financial conflicts of interest were declared in one report. Nine reports received "lower quality" or "lowest quality" research quality judgements. Six reports received "high risk of bias" judgements. Bias risk was commonly associated with selective reporting of data. M. oleifera seed toxicity was commonly tested via rodent study. Seven rodent studies included an acute toxicity test and nine included a sub-acute toxicity test. Two acute oral toxicity tests returned LD50 values of 14,000-15,000 mg/kg bw. Three sub-acute oral toxicity tests returned NOAEL values of 100-257 mg/kg bw/d. Oral LD50 and NOAEL data could only be derived from reports with "lowest quality" research and/or "high risk of bias" judgements, so these safety limits are unreliable. Inadequate dosing schemes were the primary cause of limited LD50 and NOAEL data. Dose range non-compliance also caused unnecessary animal suffering. To facilitate standardisation in future research, several guideline-based methodological recommendations are made. Determining reliable safety limits for M. oleifera seed consumption may reduce incidence of acute kidney injury, thereby supporting Targets 3.4 and 3.d of the United Nations sustainable development goals.

title: Effects of vitamin D supplementation on vitamin D status and physical performance in football players: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

grader.main_outcome: physical performance (jump, sprint, aerobic, muscular) in football players
grader.population: association football and futsal players

label: approved
note: Physical performance has four pooled outcomes, all non-significant; jump listed first; low certainty.
abstract:
Background/objectives

Low vitamin D status is frequently reported among athletes, but whether vitamin D supplementation improves physical performance in football players remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of vitamin D supplementation on serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] concentration, jump performance, sprint performance, aerobic capacity, and muscular performance in association football and futsal players.

Methods

PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 31 May 2026. Controlled intervention studies comparing vitamin D supplementation with control conditions were eligible. Standardized mean differences were calculated as Hedges' g and pooled using random-effects meta-analyses. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2 or ROBINS-I. The certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261430873).

Results

Eleven reports representing nine independent studies and 312 players were included. In RCT-only primary analyses, vitamin D supplementation was associated with higher circulating 25(OH)D concentrations (g = 1.41, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.92; I² = 58.0%). Pooled effects were not statistically significant for jump performance (g = 0.21, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.53), sprint performance (g = -0.03, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.34), aerobic capacity (g = 0.00, 95% CI -0.45 to 0.45), or muscular performance (g = 0.19, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.51). The certainty of evidence was low for circulating 25(OH)D, jump performance, and muscular performance, and very low for sprint performance and aerobic capacity.

Conclusions

Vitamin D supplementation was associated with increased circulating 25(OH)D concentrations, whereas current evidence is insufficient to support a consistent improvement in physical performance. Given the low to very low certainty of evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Larger, well-designed randomized controlled trials using standardized, football-relevant performance tests are warranted.

title: Oral Acarbose Inhibits Baseline Salivary Amylase and Blunts Early Postprandial Glycemia: Randomized Cross-Over Study.

grader.main_outcome: early postprandial blood glucose rise
grader.population: healthy young women

label: approved
note: P values only.
abstract:
Unlabelled

This study investigated whether salivary α-amylase (SAA) inhibition by acarbose affects postprandial blood glucose (BG) in healthy individuals. This single-blinded, placebo-controlled, randomized cross-over trial included 4 conditions: trial 1 (T1), placebo (oligosaccharide); trial 2 (T2), swallowing 50 mg of acarbose; and trials 3 and 4 (T3 and T4), simultaneous intake of starch (150 g of rice) with 50 mg or 100 mg of acarbose, respectively. Fifteen young, healthy women were enrolled. Peak ΔBG occurred at 30 min in both T1 and T2 and at 60 min in T3. ΔBG at 30 min was significantly lower in T3 and T4 than in T2 (both P<.05) without trial order effect, while BG areas under the curve did not differ between T2 and T3. Inhibition of SAA by oral acarbose reduced the early postprandial increase in BG compared with intact SAA activity in healthy individuals.

title: Effect of continuous high thermal processing on physico-chemical and nutritional alterations in cold-pressed and refined edible oils.

grader.main_outcome: oxidative and chemical changes in edible oils under continuous heating

label: approved
note: Oil chemistry under heating; values, no effect measure.
abstract:
Background

Continuous high thermal processing of edible oils induces significant physicochemical and nutritional alterations, influence their safety, stability, and consumer acceptability. Cold-pressed oils are generally perceived as nutritionally superior, but their oxidative stability under continuous heating remains less understand compared to the refined oils.

Methods

Twelve edible oils (7 cold-pressed and 5 refined oils) were collected and subjected to the continuous high thermal processing at 230 ± 5 °C for 0, 1, 2, and 4 h. Fatty acid composition, peroxide value, saponification value, free fatty acid percentage, acid value, iodine value, conjugated dienes, conjugated trienes, refractive index and colour were analysed.

Results

Among the oils available in the both cold-pressed and refined types, cold-pressed groundnut, sunflower, rice bran and palm oil retained more polyunsaturated fatty acids at 1 h, but showed greater losses after 4 h then their refined types. Soybean oil exhibited a sharp rise in trans fatty acids (0.76 to 5.88%), whereas, coconut oil remained lowest (0.38%) at 4 h. Peroxide value increased in refined sunflower oil (7.60 to 15.81 mEq O2/kg), but refined and cold-pressed rice bran oil declined to 0.01 mEq O2/kg in after 2 h. Free fatty acid and acid values decreased variably across oils. Iodine value reduction was highest in coconut oil and minimal in soybean oil (6.72%). Saponification peaked in coconut oil (321 ± 0.68 mg KOH/g) and lowest in cold-pressed sunflower oil (213 ± 0.83 mg KOH/g). Conjugated triene rose steadily but remained below diene, while progressive darkening (L* reduction) was observed in all oils. Heating for 1 to 2 h impacted the saturation of fatty acids, while 4 h can increase the risk of trans fatty acid and dienes/trienes formation.

Conclusion

Continuous high thermal processing compromises the nutritional and oxidative stability of edible oils. Coconut oil showed minimal alterations, while soybean oil and sesame oil were highly susceptible. These findings highlight the need for cautious thermal application in cooking practices to preserve oil quality.

title: Self-Care Practices Among Adults With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus in Urban and Rural Areas of Bhubaneswar, India.

grader.main_outcome: self-care practices (diet, exercise, glucose monitoring) by urban and rural residence
grader.population: adults with type 2 diabetes in Bhubaneswar, India, urban and rural

label: approved
note: p values only.
abstract:
Background

Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a rapidly growing public health problem, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Effective self-care practices are essential for optimal glycemic control and prevention of complications. Urbanization has introduced lifestyle and health system-related challenges that may differentially influence diabetes self-care behaviors.

Objectives

The objective of the study is to assess self-care practices among adults with T2DM in Bhubaneswar and to compare these practices between urban and rural populations.

Methods

A community-based study was conducted from December 2020 to September 2022 among 465 adults with T2DM using multistage cluster sampling. The study design was cross-sectional. Self-care practices were assessed using the Summary of Diabetes Self-Care Activities (SDSCA) scale. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Chi-squared test, Fisher's exact test, and crude odds ratio were reported.

Results

Poor dietary habits (p = 0.035) and exercise behaviors (p = 0.018) were significantly more prevalent among urban participants, while rural participants demonstrated better blood glucose monitoring (p = 0.001). Residence showed a significant association with multiple dimensions of self-care. Women had significantly less smoking habit (p = 0.005). Poor dietary habits (p = 0.001) were significantly more prevalent among participants with uncontrolled blood sugar, whereas poor exercise, although more prevalent, was not statistically significant (p = 0.080) in the same group.

Conclusion

Urban residents exhibited poorer lifestyle-related self-care behaviors despite better healthcare access, highlighting the need for targeted urban diabetes interventions. Poor dietary and exercise habits are common lapses in self-care behavior and should be more emphasized.

title: Optimization of ultrasound-assisted extraction of polyphenols from <i>Mansoa alliacea</i> flowers and evaluation of their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory-related, and digestive enzyme inhibitory activities.

grader.main_outcome: in vitro antioxidant and enzyme inhibitory activity of flower extract

label: approved
note: In vitro; IC50 values, no effect measure; 'preliminary scientific support' is a stated caution.
abstract:
Background

Mansoa alliacea is traditionally used to treat inflammation, infections, and metabolic disorders. However, the phytochemical and biological potential of its flowers remains poorly characterized.

Purpose

This study optimized ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE) of polyphenols from M. alliacea flowers and evaluated the in vitro antioxidant, anti-inflammatory-related, and digestive enzyme inhibitory activities of the optimized extract.

Methods

Four extraction parameters (ethanol concentration, extraction temperature, extraction time, and solid-to-solvent ratio) were initially screened by single-factor experiments. Based on these results, three key factors (temperature, time, and ethanol concentration) were selected and further optimized using a Box-Behnken design to maximize polyphenol yield. Total polyphenol content was quantified using the Folin-Ciocalteu method. UHPLC-MS profiling was conducted for tentative phytochemical characterization. The optimized extract was evaluated for in vitro antioxidant activity (DPPH, ABTS assays), anti-inflammatory activity (protein denaturation and RBC membrane stabilization), and digestive enzyme inhibitory activities (inhibition of α-amylase and α-glucosidase).

Results

Optimal extraction conditions (60% ethanol, 79 °C, 15 min, 1:10 w/v) yielded 275.37 ± 1.55 mg GAE/g extract. UHPLC-MS analysis revealed nine major peaks, among which two compounds were provisionally assigned as luteolin-7-O-glucoside and luteolin-7-O-glucuronide. Compared with the unoptimized extract, the optimized extract exhibited markedly stronger in vitro biological activities, with IC50 values of 11.88 ± 0.28 and 15.58 ± 0.33 μg/mL in DPPH and ABTS assays, respectively; 38.77 ± 0.93 μg/mL for inhibition of protein denaturation; 30.74 ± 0.18 μg/mL for RBC membrane stabilization; and 30.94 ± 0.54 and 13.32 ± 0.19 μg/mL for α-amylase and α-glucosidase inhibition, respectively.

Conclusion

Optimized UAE significantly enhanced polyphenol enrichment in the extract and improved the in vitro antioxidant capacity, protective effects against protein denaturation and RBC hemolysis, and carbohydrate-hydrolyzing enzyme inhibitory activities of M. alliacea flower extract. These findings provide preliminary scientific support for the traditional use of M. alliacea and suggest that its polyphenol-rich extract may serve as a promising candidate for further investigation as a functional or phytopharmaceutical ingredient.
